articles.title: Linen: The Wrinkly Fabric That Gave Us the Word 'Line'
paragraphs: Next time you draw a straight line, you can thank a flax plant. The word "line" comes from the old practice of using linen thread to mark something straight, and it is just one of the sneaky ways linen has woven itself into English.

Linen is a textile made from the bast fibers of the flax plant, and it is one of the oldest fabrics we know of. Dyed flax fibers found in a cave in present-day Georgia date back about 36,000 years, hinting that people were making linen-like cloth very early. Ancient Egyptians wore white linen every day and wrapped their mummies in it as a symbol of light and purity. The Tarkhan dress, made of linen and dated to between 3482 and 3102 BC, is considered one of the oldest woven garments in the world.

Why has it lasted so long in our closets? Linen is strong, absorbent, and dries faster than cotton, so it feels comfortable in hot weather. It can be up to three times stronger than cotton, because its cellulose fibers are slightly longer and wrapped tighter. It even feels cool to the touch. Moths and carpet beetles leave it alone, since it isn't made from animal fibers. Its famous drawback is wrinkling, though fans consider that part of its charm.

Making it takes patience. Flax needs a great deal of attention, and linen takes longer to harvest and process than cotton and is harder to weave. The thread has little elasticity, which is why linen costs considerably more to make.

Linen has also built whole towns. After many Huguenots fled France in 1685, they brought improved methods to Ireland, and the town of Lisburn became so dominant in the Victorian era that it earned the nickname Linenopolis. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, linen was Russia's greatest export at one time, and the country grew about 80% of the world's fiber flax.

Linen has worked in some surprising jobs, too. Ancient warriors wore linen body armor called a linothorax, and sailors loved linen ropes and sails because the cloth grows about 20% stronger when wet. Artisan bakers still rest dough on floured linen cloths. And if you carry U.S. dollars, you are carrying linen: the paper is 25% linen and 75% cotton.
